questions.question_text: Rewrite $\operatorname{cosec} 52^{\circ}$ as the secant of an acute angle.

options.why: Replaced cosecant with secant without subtracting the angle from $90^{\circ}$.
Subtracted from $90^{\circ}$ but kept the original cosecant ratio instead of swapping to secant.
Subtracted from $180^{\circ}$ instead of using the complementary angle sum of $90^{\circ}$.

questions.question_text: Rewrite $\cot 41^{\circ}$ as the tangent of an acute angle.

options.why: Subtracted the angle from $180^{\circ}$ rather than $90^{\circ}$, giving $139^{\circ}$.
Found the complement $49^{\circ}$ but forgot to swap cotangent to tangent.
Made both slips: used $180^{\circ}-41^{\circ}$ and also left the ratio as cotangent.
Evaluated only the first quotient and omitted the subtraction of the second quotient.
Added the two quotients instead of subtracting the second from the first.
Inverted the signs of both quotients during evaluation.
Assumed numerator and denominator are equal without converting both cofunctions.
Inverted the cofunction substitutions for numerator and denominator.
Simplified the quotient as a single power instead of dividing $\cot\alpha$ by $\tan\alpha$.

questions.question_text: Find the value of acute angle $\theta$ in degrees if $\cot(3\theta+12^{\circ}) = \tan(2\theta+18^{\circ})$.

options.why: Set $3\theta+12^{\circ} = 2\theta+18^{\circ}$ instead of equating their sum to $90^{\circ}$.
Added the angle constants incorrectly when subtracting from $90^{\circ}$.
Equated the sum of the angles to $180^{\circ}$ instead of the complementary sum $90^{\circ}$.

questions.question_text: Find the value of acute angle $y$ in degrees if $\sec(4y-10^{\circ}) = \operatorname{cosec}(y+25^{\circ})$.

options.why: Set $4y-10^{\circ} = y+25^{\circ}$ assuming equal arguments rather than complementary angles.
Added $15^{\circ}$ to $90^{\circ}$ instead of subtracting when isolating $5y$.
Used a supplementary angle sum of $180^{\circ}$ instead of complementary $90^{\circ}$.

questions.question_text: Which algebraic step correctly begins the proof of $\cot(90^{\circ}-\theta) = \tan\theta$ using ratio and complementary identities?

options.text: Multiply both sides by $\tan(90^{\circ}-\theta)$ to clear fractions.
options.why: Applies operations to both sides of the statement being proven instead of transforming one side.

options.text: Replace $\cot(90^{\circ}-\theta)$ with $\dfrac{1}{\cos(90^{\circ}-\theta)}$ using the reciprocal identity.
options.why: Confused the cotangent ratio definition with the secant reciprocal identity.

options.text: Substitute $\theta = 45^{\circ}$ into both sides to verify equality.
options.why: Testing a single numerical value is an empirical check rather than a general algebraic proof.

questions.question_text: Solve $\sec(2x+15^{\circ}) = \operatorname{cosec}(x+30^{\circ})$ for acute $x$, and hence determine the exact value of $\cot(3x)$.

options.why: Evaluated $\cot(x)$ at $15^{\circ}$ or misapplied the exact ratio for $30^{\circ}$.
Evaluated $\tan(3x)$ as $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ instead of finding $\cot(45^{\circ})=1$.
Substituted $x=15^{\circ}$ into $\cos(3x)$ rather than evaluating the cotangent ratio.

questions.solution_text:
Since $\sec A = \operatorname{cosec} B$, the angles are complementary.
$(2x+15^{\circ}) + (x+30^{\circ}) = 90^{\circ}$
$3x + 45^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$
$3x = 45^{\circ}$
$x = 15^{\circ}$
$\cot(3x) = \cot(45^{\circ})$
$= 1$
